paragraphs.text: ReNU syndrome is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder. Its main features are moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, seizures and motor delay. Many patients have absent or very limited speech, distinctive facial features, abnormalities on brain MRI, and involvement of other organ systems. The disorder is caused by heterozygous, usually de novo, variants in a short critical region of RNU4-2, which encodes the U4 small nuclear RNA (snRNA) of the major spliceosome (Greene et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024).

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) analyzed Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms in 46 cases from the UK 100,000 Genomes Project (100KGP) who had RNU4-2 variants and were coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality. Intellectual disability (91%), neurodevelopmental delay (91%) and motor delay (61%) occurred at rates broadly similar to those in other intellectual disability cases. Several terms were significantly overrepresented compared with other neurodevelopmental cases: microcephaly (57% vs 18%), drooling (13% vs 1%), proportionate short stature (28% vs 7%), generalized hypotonia (39% vs 13%), seizures (52% vs 27%) and abnormality of the upper lip vermilion (13% vs 2%). No terms were significantly underrepresented.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) also collected detailed phenotypic data on 49 individuals with RNU4-2 variants: 21 females and 28 males, with a median age of 10 years (range 2-38 years). Forty-two carried n.64_65insT, 3 carried other single-base insertions and 4 carried single-nucleotide variants (SNVs). All had moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability. Of those older than 5 years, 83% walked, at an average age of 3.4 years, and some had a wide-based or ataxic gait. Most were nonverbal, and only 3 had fluent speech. Other frequent features were: - hypotonia (87%) - microcephaly (77%, mostly congenital) - short stature (76%) - seizures (77%) - abnormal brain MRI (91%) - vision problems (79%) - feeding difficulties (76%) - constipation (66%) - behavioral problems (67%) - autism spectrum disorder (48%) Forty-five of 48 individuals had dysmorphic facial features. These varied but included a myopathic face with deep-set eyes (some widely and some narrowly spaced), epicanthus, a wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares or underdeveloped alae nasi, large cupped ears (some posteriorly rotated), full cheeks, full lips with downturned corners, a high-arched palate and a large or protruding tongue.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) identified 8 rare RNU4-2 variants that occurred only in affected participants. The variants lay in two contiguous regions, n.62-70 and n.73-79, in which no unaffected participant carried a rare variant; these regions sit within a locus markedly depleted of variation in gnomAD. Among the 47 cases with a variant in these regions, the variant was de novo in 37, and its inheritance was unknown in 10 because parental genotypes were missing. The variants map either to the U4 quasi-pseudoknot (n.63T>G, n.64_65insG, n.64_65insT, n.65A>G, n.65_66insT, n.67A>G, n.68_69insA) or to U4 stem III (n.76C>T, n.77_78insT). The authors predicted that they destabilize the interaction of U4 with U6 snRNA. The most common variant, n.64_65insT, had arisen de novo in 33 different families. paragraphs.text: The most frequent variant identified by Chen et al. (2024) was the highly recurrent single-base insertion n.64_65insT, which lies within the T-loop structure. paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) noted that RNU4-2 encodes the U4 snRNA component of the U4 snRNP, one of the five snRNPs of the major spliceosome. GTEx RNA-seq data showed that RNU4-2, like many major spliceosome components, is ubiquitously expressed across adult tissues. Using published secondary-structure data, the authors found that one variant region maps to the quasi-pseudoknot interaction between U4 and U6 snRNA and the other maps to the U4-U6 stem III interaction. The G at position 64 of U4 snRNA is thought to help stabilize the ACAGAGA loop of U6 snRNA, and n.64_65insT could disrupt the G64(U4)-A47(U6) interaction that supports the quasi-pseudoknot. Biallelic loss-of-function variants in WBP4, a spliceosome protein that delays U4-U6 unwinding by SNRNP200, cause a strikingly similar syndrome. The authors therefore suggested that a delay in U4-U6 unwinding might be the underlying disease mechanism.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) noted that the 18-bp critical region of U4 lies between stem I and the 3-prime stem-loops. This region is loaded into the active site of the BRR2 helicase (encoded by SNRNP200), which unwinds the U4/U6 duplex during spliceosome activation. The T-loop ('quasi pseudoknot') containing n.64_65insT and the stem III region containing n.77_78insT are both thought to stabilize U4/U6 pairing and to position the U6 ACAGAGA sequence to receive the 5-prime splice site. The authors suggested that single-base insertions may destabilize the U4/U6 interaction or alter positioning of the ACAGAGA sequence. They performed RNA-seq on blood from 5 GEL individuals: 3 with n.64_65insT, 1 with n.77_78insT and 1 with n.78A>C. Compared with controls, these individuals showed significantly increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites (mean 8.8 vs 0.7 events). Twelve abnormal splicing events were shared by 2 or more affected individuals and absent from all 378 controls, and 11 of these involved unannotated 5-prime splice sites. The sites with increased use showed shifts away from consensus at positions +3, +4 and +5, which pair with U6 ACAGAGA. The authors concluded that RNU4-2 variants systematically disrupt 5-prime splice-site recognition.

checks.claim: RNU4-2 n.77_78insT lies in the region spanning nucleotides 76 to 78 of U4, which base-pairs with U6 snRNA in stem III.
checks.evidence_quote: The region spanning nucleotides 76 to 78, where the recurrent n.77_78insT variant resides, is involved in base pairing with U6 in stem III

checks.claim: RNA-seq of blood from 1 carrier of RNU4-2 n.77_78insT, analyzed together with 4 carriers of other RNU4-2 variants, showed increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites compared with controls.
checks.evidence_quote: Three of these individuals have the highly recurrent n.64_65insT variant, another has the other recurrent insertion, n.77_78insT and the final individual has an SNV (n.78A>C).
checks.explanation: The group of five showed significantly increased use of unannotated 5′ splice sites compared with controls.

checks.claim: RNA-seq of blood from 1 carrier of RNU4-2 n.78A-C, analyzed together with 4 carriers of RNU4-2 insertions, showed significantly increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites compared with controls.
checks.evidence_quote: The individual with the SNV was not notably different from the four individuals with single base insertions (three significant events).
checks.explanation: The group of five, including this individual and four with insertions, showed significantly increased use of unannotated 5′ splice sites.
